examples.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={x}^{2}(t)+3y(t)-4x(t)+4 \\ {y}^{′}(t)={x}^{2}(t)-2x(t)+{y}^{2}(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the corresponding linearized system at the equilibrium point $\mathbf{x}^\ast=[2, \ 0]^T?$
examples.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
\mathbf{x}' = \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x})
$$

where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094758/assets/3778afde5f90cb0f7d0ac6cfe75a38e790d3c29ac5b16148ff997bc5e2d618b6.png) and 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094758/assets/bda68b8ced804286f348d4ba16e62fd98461be02c9a93974fa328f96fc650597.png)

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094758/assets/edc462937a0fd6be62bc13a9ef9ec02640c374eec382e5f0a69b08c08ef1b72f.png)

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+3y-4x+4)=2x-4,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+3y-4x+4)=3 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-2x+{y}^{2})=2x-2,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-2x+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094758/assets/7a5e0413bd5830d067ee908e054f4e8f9949a464ea93587fc9a0b61897f7c420.png)

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094758/assets/e42f71d062ff514ebcb1c2abefea9d4174896d4b67f52da8a67c99c2e79a4d24.png) to get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094758/assets/8ffda98648f540450a8071dda6f20208768e35c7f0858936f5e17379381c00dd.png)

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094758/assets/1153c649732a1fad021e0118b5779e55f3b18de5958479088343770d1b8f95bc.png)

where the deviation vector is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094758/assets/4369f0ba7e84c6e3a9fc540b1395fdb74ee74eb50d895fac0428dfb9cd8abe27.png)

$$

Given the system of differential equations, select the correct options below.The Jacobian determinant of the system at the equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}=[1,\text{ }1]^{T}$ is given as

J(1,1)={{field-1}}.

feedback.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y) \\ {y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of $f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}|
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y))=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y))=-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y) \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x))=-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x),\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x))=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}2x & -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y) \\ -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x) & 2y\end{aligned}|.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}J(1,1) & =|\begin{aligned}2(1) & -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi (1)) \\ -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi (1)) & 2(1)\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot 2-0\cdot 0 \\  & =4 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is not zero, our system is $\text{almost linear}$ at ${x}^{∗}.$
